Mr. Speaker, there is no doubt that the unemployment situation is a serious matter and demands that every hon. member should shoulder his or her responsibility. Many hon. members have emphasized the importance of this debate on unemployment, but I would say that this debate is important only if it brings about some solution and some relief in the way of immediate action as far as unemployment is concerned.
Perhaps the anticipation of what might be said in this debate has caused the government to do some research work to find out whether they can defend their position rather than to find a solution to the problem before us. I do not think that the government is too proud of its record, and I need not dwell on that part of the problem. I do not think they are too proud of their stewardship. In spite of all that has been said by the ministers, it does not obscure the fact that they did allow the situation to develop, and therefore to that extent at least the government is responsible.
We recognize that we have a problem. Therefore, what matters most is, what are we going to do about it rather than who is to blame? We must deal with the unemployment problem first, and let the people decide on the other question when the time comes.

Unemployment
As a member from British Columbia, naturally I am more concerned about the conditions there than elsewhere in Canada. Naturally, too, I am more familiar with what is being done to meet the unemployment problem in that province.
As far back as July of last year the premier of British Columbia approached the Prime Minister with respect to holding a dominion-provincial conference to discuss unemployment. This approach was acknowledged, and there the matter rested. We were pleased to hear that there is a possibility of such a conference taking place later this year, but that does not help the unemployment situation at this time.
The minister of labour of the province of British Columbia came to grips with the problem of unemployment and instituted the holding of a series of conferences with representatives of organized labour, employers' organizations, boards of trade, and so on, for the purpose of getting suggestions as to what might be done, and to what extent unemployment could be curbed. The Vancouver board of trade went into the problem and came up with some suggestions which I believe were both constructive and helpful, as did other organizations. Perhaps I can put on the record a summary of their recommendations, which appeared under two headings:
1.	Destitution:	The relief of destitution when
such exists is a proper function of government. We note that the special arrangements made last year between the provincial government and the municipal governments are being continued. This committee recommends even closer liaison between the federal, provincial and municipal authorities for the relief of destitution.
2.	Employment: Primary constructive action relating to fluctuations in employment must originate with the main spending groups in the province which are federal government, including crown companies, commissions and boards:	provincial
government, including commissions and boards; municipal and local governments, including commissions and boards; industry and commerce, and the individual citizen.
The British Columbia government have increased their expenditures on public works, such as school construction, the building and extension of hospitals and new hospitals, the building of bridges, the extension of the Pacific Great Eastern Railway, and many other projects, to meet the problem of unemployment, and also to carry on the development of the province. Assistance to municipalities on an 80-20 basis is given toward the cost of relief and welfare.
Much emphasis was placed on the importance of instituting as much construction and repairs as possible during the winter months. The industries throughout the province were circularized and urged to discontinue as much as possible the payment for and the use of

overtime. This of course would not be possible in all cases, particularly in the lumber camps where the operators have to provide board and lodging for their employees. It can be well understood that if additional men were to be hired, additional bunk houses and services would have to be provided and therefore some operators might find it impossible to provide that type of service. Those industries which have no responsibility for housing or feeding their employees can participate in the regulation of overtime.
We also find that the government extended their technical training program under which return transportation was provided and a subsistence allowance of $14 a week was paid while the students were attending school. In this connection, training has already commenced for welders who will be required in the construction of the new gas pipe line from the Peace river country.
While British Columbia contributes more than 9 per cent of the total income tax paid to Ottawa, the co-operation of the dominion government in the matter of unemployment is sadly lacking. We know that the responsibility for unemployment rests with the federal government, since the federal government controls and has authority over the issuance of credit and currency within Canada. Unemployment can only be solved completely by a sound and sane federal financial policy. Therefore, it is unfair for this government to suggest that no financial help need be given to provinces until they can prove that they are not financially able to look after those unemployed who happen to be within their borders.
I should like to state that the British Columbia division of the Canadian Manufacturers Association highly commended the British Columbia government for what they had done to avoid an unemployment situation. This same body also emphasized the need for the federal government to allocate a fair proportion of the defence orders to the firms in the province of British Columbia,
Coming down to the individual we find a rather complex situation. It would mean much in the way of assistance to the unemployed if many repair and maintenance jobs were carried out during the winter months; but the fact is that when individuals are laid off at various times throughout the winter months they are put in a position where they can do many of the things which they would ordinarily ask someone else to come in to do for them, such as painting, carpentry work, automobile repairs and so on. Ordinarily they would go down to the local garage to get this work done, but when they are out of work themselves they do it at home

to save that'expense. This has a direct effect upon the situation as it pertains to carpenters, painters, automobile repair men, mechanics and so on.
This brings us to the point where we must look at the problem in a broad way. There is no immediate solution to this problem outside of getting down to a sane and sound financial policy. When he replies I should like the minister to pay special attention to the program outlined by the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Johnston) and to the way in which that program can be brought into being as mentioned in the speech of the hon. member for Acadia (Mr. Quelch). If the minister will analyse that program and how it can be fulfilled I think he will find it difficult to show the house that it cannot be carried out. I want to stress that point because I think that the solution to the unemployment situation is a sound federal financial policy.

Mr. Speaker, in rising to take part in this unemployment debate I do so with a feeling, which is shared by the majority of the people of Canada, that a crisis has arisen in our unemployment situation which has not been equalled at any time prior to the second world war. To bear that out I should like to refer to an article which appeared this week in the Montreal Gazette. This concerned a study of the unemployment situation made by the Montreal presbytery of the United Church of Canada and covering the unemployment situation in that city. Among other things they say that many families are in dire need and their number is increasing.
They go on to say that the situation is actually so serious that every effort must be made to inform the Canadian people who are living in relative prosperity that a considerable group of their fellow citizens is out of work and that many more will be facing a similar tragedy if immediate action is not taken to increase employment.
The unemployment situation in Canada is now a serious reality. We cannot be lulled into a false sense of security by being told that it is of a temporary or seasonal nature. This situation which has existed since the early part of 1952 has gradually increased despite all efforts by numerous spokesmen on the government side to minimize the situation and explain it away by saying that in the very near future it will right itself.
During this debate we have listened to the minister quote figures in connection with this problem in an effort to alleviate the feelings of the people of Canada and to convince them that things probably are not as bad as they seem. I think we are wasting time 50433-108
Unemployment
by quoting figures. What is needed is some drastic action on the part of the government rather than the quoting of any figures.
During the period of time that this unemployment situation has gradually increased, no visible effort has been made by the government to alleviate the condition or to provide safeguards against its increase. Consequently we find ourselves with unemployment on a scale of national emergency and with no solution proposed by the government to take care of the hundreds of thousands who are presently unemployed.
This matter of unemployment has been brought to the attention of the government by many organizations who have shown an interest in the welfare of the people of Canada, only to be turned away with some excuse and without any assurance that the government was prepared to meet this problem. The government says that it is concerned with the problem but in no way does it offer any solution nor does it commit itself to do anything at the present time regarding this problem.
Responsible labour organizations and others have stated that unemployment is the problem of the federal government, and with this everyone will agree even though the government in its statements to these delegations had said clearly that the responsibility lies with the provincial governments, that the provincial governments should take the initial step in advising the federal government that a state of unemployment exists in Canada.
I do not agree with that at all because I have found that when the government has been faced with many problems which have come before it and which concern the people of Canada they seem to use that same excuse time and time again. The federal government should take the lead in a problem as large as this one, because it is the senior government and the responsibility for that problem lies directly on the federal government.
On reviewing the economic situation in Canada we find that in most cases the reason for unemployment is that industries are unable to compete with imported goods. The farmer's income has been lowered greatly because of import competition and the spending capacity of the farmer has been limited to bare necessities.
Unemployment has always presented a problem in relief. The government which bears the brunt of this expenditure is of course the municipal government, the government which in comparison with the senior provincial and federal governments is the least able to take care of this problem.

Unemployment
I feel that it is time for both the municipal and provincial governments to take necessary steps to lay the responsibility for relief where in no small degree it properly belongs, on the federal government. Neither the municipal nor provincial governments can exert a great deal of control over the causes of unemployment, which are basically economic. The federal government is the only government which under the powers it possesses can exert control over those causes of unemployment.
It was the municipality and the municipal taxpayer which bore the heavy brunt during the days when depression was rampant in Canada. It was many years before some of them were able to emerge from the state of bankruptcy in which they found themselves because of this responsibility. With the situation as it is at the present time I feel that it will be only a matter of time before they will again find themselves in the same position.
I feel it is at this time that the municipal and provincial governments should adopt a policy of doing nothing about the present situation in order to force the federal government to take the responsibility which is rightly theirs. Provincial and municipal governments do not shape national policies. It is the federal government which holds that responsibility and it is national policy which determines employment or unemployment. It is the federal government which takes from the Canadian taxpayer's pocket the largest share of the Canadian tax dollar, leaving only a small percentage to the overburdened municipality. The federal government takes well over 77 per cent of the tax dollar, leaving something like 12 per cent for the provincial government and only 11 per cent for the municipalities.
We find that real estate taxes in various municipalities have had to be increased time and time again in order to meet the necessary rise in the costs of municipal administration for the provision of services which are extremely necessary such as health, hospitals, education, etc. In most cases they have reached the point where municipal taxes are almost unbearable and this leaves the worried and harassed municipalities at road's end.
The municipal authorities are closest to the people and necessarily feel the plight of the people to a greater extent than those who are in the federal field and who seem to be divorced from the requirements of the ordinary citizen.
Recently when an amendment to the Unemployment Insurance Act was introduced in this house to raise the supplementary benefits

to the scale of regular benefits the hon. members on this side of the house urged that the time in which these supplementary benefits would be available should be extended to another 30 days at least. It would certainly have helped the municipalities in the matter of supplying relief and would have lessened the time during which these people would have been a burden on the municipality by at least a meagre 30 days but the government did not feel that it was in a position to implement this suggestion.
Not too long ago in this house it was announced that a federal-provincial conference will be held some time in June, at which time one of the matters brought before this conference might possibly be the question of financial responsibility during a period of unemployment. However, June is a long way off and unemployment is with us today in full force. It is obvious therefore that a conference on this particular subject should be called now in order to arrive at some conclusive plan to deal with this serious problem. Because of the lack of action on the part of the federal government at this time concerning the unemployment situation, the onus for taking care of those people whose benefits under the Unemployment Insurance Act have run out falls upon the municipalities. With the increasing debenture debts which the municipalities have had to undertake in the post-war years they are not in a position to budget large amounts of money to supplement a situation which the federal government has created through its policies. It is up to the federal government to do everything in its power to provide for the immediate needs of the unemployed of this country and to provide safeguards for the time when any future unemployment may occur. This situation demands drastic and immediate action. Those Canadians who are faced with unemployment and the lack of necessities to provide for themselves and their families will not accept the excuse that this is a seasonal occurrence.
I am amazed at the stand taken by this government which appears to be a policy of "wait and see". It seems to me that the government should give some hope to the people of Canada by assuring them that it is planning and preparing to take care of their immediate needs and is implementing safeguards for the prevention of future situations of this kind.
Unemployment has reached a figure of close to 600,000 and this is indeed an alarming figure. It is not a situation which can be brushed aside nor can the problem be shifted to another level of government. It is a problem which only the senior government

of this country can tackle effectively providing they feel, as they should, that the responsibility is theirs.
It is to be hoped that this debate does not fall on deaf ears. I am sure that the government itself realizes the seriousness of the problem and the hardships which are being experienced by the people of Canada who are at present affected by unemployment. For this reason I urge the Minister of Labour (Mr. Gregg) to formulate some comprehensive plan which will cope with the situation and eliminate unemployment in this country. If this is done it will alleviate the fears of the municipal councils throughout Canada that they may be called upon to bear the brunt of this financial burden. It will reassure those who are unfortunate enough to be unemployed that they will be looked after by this responsible government and that the government is sincerely endeavouring to work out a solution to the problem of their unemployment.
Unemployment insurance cannot meet the needs of all the unemployed because many wage earners are not in insured occupations. Many have been unemployed for so long that they have exhausted all their benefits including the supplementary benefits. There are others among the unemployed who have not had an opportunity to fulfil the requirements under the act in order to receive unemployment insurance benefits. There are others to whom help from public funds is not available at present. We find the heads of many families who are unemployed are denied help by municipal authorities on the ground that they are employable. In most cases these people are referred from one charitable organization to another and they are forced to beg for clothes and groceries for their families. These charitable organizations cannot be expected to provide continued security for these people but in most cases they are ready and willing to help those in desperate circumstances on a temporary basis.
The important thing at the present time is to place the blame and the responsibility for unemployment on the proper government. Delegation after delegation is becoming fed up with the shirking of responsibility on the part of this government. We must place the responsibility with the federal government where it belongs. It is the senior government which must take the lead in respect to any national problem. Unemployment definitely comes within that category.
Mr. Speaker, I hope that this debate will not be wasted time and that the Minister of 50433-108J
Unemployment
Labour and his colleagues will announce at once a plan to end unemployment in Canada and assure the people that action will be forthcoming immediately.

Mr. Speaker, the amendment now before the house is, to my mind, about the most fantastic than can be imagined. On looking at it, I find one sentence in particular reading as follows:
In the opinion of this house . . . the government should immediately give consideration to the formulation of plans to deal with this emergency-
Any member who has been sitting here since the opening of this parliament could hardly be unaware of the many measures introduced by the government to deal with the present situation. It will nevertheless be recognized-and I may discuss this point later on-that responsibility for employment does not rest on the federal government alone. Still, in view of the many steps taken by this government in the past few years to improve the past or present situation, I feel it can be stated that no business, no organization, no government has done as much as the federal government for the betterment of the employment situation in this country.
In the splendid statements made by the Minister of Labour (Mr. Gregg) and the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) we have had a review of federal action in this field. As a matter of fact we were even given a picture of the conditions which prevail at present in this country. I was happy to learn, from the leader of the official opposition himself (Mr. Drew), that Canada's position was healthy and that we should be happy to live here, especially since the administration is at present in Liberal hands.
No one is attempting to gloss over the unemployment situation. All members in this house recognize, I am sure, that it is indeed a problem requiring the co-operation of everyone and I believe it is the duty, not only of the federal government, but of every level of government, provincial and municipal as well and even of civil organizations, to help solve the problem.
A few days ago, the premier of Ontario himself admitted that the provinces share the responsibility as regards employment in Canada. On the other hand, the premier of Quebec stated on the last day of the session which ended last week that unemployment was a federal responsibility. Fortunately, he is the only one to voice that opinion. All others seem to recognize that not only the federal government but all provincial governments, and I base this statement upon the

Unemployment
British North America Act, share a measure OB responsibility in the adjustment of such a situation. My opinion is that the co-operation which the various groups and the various governments have shown in the past should be intensified. I do not believe that because the -federal government took the initiative, some fifteen years ago, of creating the unemployment insurance commission and of voting millions of dollars for relief to the unemployed, it should now be held solely responsible for the present situation.. On the contrary, all Canadians of good will, all organizations in the country should continue to co-operate in seeking a solution to the problem.
I shall not go over the many measures taken by this government to relieve the present situation. The Minister of Labour said, as did several other members, that unemployment in this country is largely due to our climate. Unemployment in Canada is mainly regional and seasonal, and I do not think we will ever find a solution which would enable us to say that we have done away with unemployment in our country. It is unfortunate but I do not believe that it can be done, in view of conditions and the climate, but I believe that if the efforts to which I Referred a while ago were intensified, we could perhaps achieve, at certain periods, a further reduction in the number of unemployed.
Besides action taken by this government, we have also had action by private organizations and provincial governments. I do not feel I have to analyse what the provincial governments may have done in this field. I do think, however, that I should put a few Suggestions before the house, not speaking directly to the federal government but to other groups in this country, so that all possible solutions to unemployment, especially winter unemployment, may be looked for.
I would first like to make a request of the newspapermen of this country, among whom may be found men quite as capable as any, wherever they may be. If they followed suit and promoted ideas, through the medium pf public forums, for instance, on every kind of subject, with a view to the solution of local and regional problems, this would improve the employment situation and, by the same token, bring about a reduction in the number of unemployed.
I also believe that one way of solving this problem-and here the federal government's responsibility is quite large-would be to
IMr. Legare.]
ensure a sufficiently high farm income so that those who are now engaged in agriculture will not be tempted to abandon that work and increase the number of those who are working in industry or business.
I think it is appropriate to mention the effects that , a reduction in the support price of butter might have in Canada. In my opinion, if this parliament were to reduce, even by a small fraction, the present support price on butter, the moral effects of such a move would be very serious. Indeed it might even drive a great number of farmers to give up their activities and to swell the ranks of the unemployed.
Our lumbering industry, and the way it operates, is another problem which demands special attention. As a matter of fact, many groups, among them our labour organizations, have made a special study of this problem. If the industry cannot operate twelve months a year, we should try to get it to operate when there is a slack in the building industry. Now in many districts, and particularly in my own, lumbering operations are often started in summer or too early in the fall, which makes it difficult to get the necessary labour. On the other hand, when felling operations are ended by Christmas or in January, or February, like this year for instance, the building industry is not ready to absorb the unemployed.
I understand that the problem has already been considered from this angle, but I believe that this study should be pursued in order to satisfy the lumber firms that our claim is justified. Those firms should be asked to operate in winter or in the fall so that the felling would only start after building operations have come to an end.
I might even make another suggestion. It might be possible to lower the wages of labour employed in construction work during the winter months, so as to balance costs for those who want to build in winter, or just make alterations or improvements to their homes.
A brief survey on the question made by labour organizations might show that a great many people would be ready to embark upon construction work even in wintertime. It must be recognized however that building is more expensive in winter than in summer. To compensate for that, it would only be necessary to lower the hourly rate of pay of workers during the cold season so that winter building would not lay too heavy a burden on those who are prepared to undertake it.

I do not wish in the least to minimize the responsibility of the government with respect to the present situation. If the federal government can do more, they must do more, and I shall be the first to ask them to make a serious attempt to solve the problem or, at least, to relieve the situation.
But I am satisfied that through joint studies and action by all well-meaning people, we could raise the population's morale, overcome the difficulties and remedy the situation so as to alleviate unemployment and give more sustained help to the unemployed.

I have no intention, Mr. Speaker, of entering into the contest as to which particular set of figures regarding the unemployed is correct. I have a suspicion that none of them is very accurate. More important still, I imagine the people who are unemployed are not very much concerned as to whether they have the company of 600,000, 500,000 or one million more when they are living in precarious misery. I believe that for a country such as Canada it is equally disgraceful whether that number be 1,000 or 600,000.
I was interested the other day when the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) was speaking in this debate and had this to say, as reported in Hansard for March 1, 1955, page 1629:
What I propose to do is to look at unemployment in relation to other important forces at work in the economy. Such an assessment is, I think, essential to arrive at a sound approach to this problem.
I could not agree more that that is what is required. Mind you, I feel it is perhaps a good idea, when one is looking at these other factors in the economy, not to look at them through rose-coloured glasses.
Just before this debate started we were all given a report from the Department of Trade and Commerce on capital investment in Canada, and it covered the years from 1947 to 1954, including an estimate for 1955. It is those figures with which I want to deal for a few moments, because they are the result of the minister's look at the other factors in our economy. I want to point out that he gives three sets of figures for current and capital investment. In 1953 there was a total capital investment of $5,841 million. Then, in 1954 there was a total capital investment of $5,498 million. The minister and his officials made an estimate of the probable investment for 1955, and that figure is set at
Unemployment
$5,808 million. We might, of course, say "WTell, things are going very well so we do not need to bother very much; our level of investment is keeping up."
Unfortunately, the year 1955 is not the only year for which the minister has produced this particular document. He produced one last year, and on that occasion he told us that the probable investment for 1954 would be $5,838 million. As a matter of fact it dropped down, as I say, to $5,498 million. There was, in fact, a decline in capital investment between the years 1953 and 1954 of 5-8 per cent, whereas the minister had estimated that there was going to be an increase of 2-5 per cent. It is quite possible, of course, for people to be mistaken in these estimates, but I do suggest that when one has been mistaken repeatedly it is time to look more cautiously at all future prognostications made by that person. I look with a very dubious eye at this estimate of possible investment in 1955 made by the minister's department. For one thing, it is not borne out by the prophecies of other people who have been making these estimates. For instance, Business Week conducted a survey of business leaders, academic economists and government economists in December 1954. Their forecast for 1955 was that investment would not exceed between $5-6 billion and $5-7 billion, not the $5-808 billion that the minister so cheerily told us would be our investment for 1955.
In addition to the decline in investment, there has been also a decline in gross national product between 1953 and 1954. It is true, as the minister pointed out, that most of it could probably be accounted for by the decline in farm production in that period. There was a decline, nevertheless, of 2-5 per cent in our gross national product. It is not merely that we have been faced with a decline in our investment and a decline in our gross national product, but we have been faced also with another problem connected with it which makes the situation very much worse than it would appear from looking at the statistical tables. During this period of declining investment and declining production, we have had an increase of 2-8 per cent in population and, more important still, a most astonishing increase in productivity.
Today 1 was able to get some figures relating to one of the industries that has been suffering from a severe decline, the agricultural implement industry. The figures proffered by this industry indicate, I think, the real nature of the problem we are facing.

Unemployment
In 1951, there were 17,236 persons employed in the agricultural implement industry, and the gross selling value of their products that year was $171,172,496. In 1953 the number employed had dropped to 14,161, a drop of nearly 6 per cent. The gross selling value of that product in that year was $171,269,525, a slight increase which is not to be accounted for incidentally by an increase in price and not to be accounted for by an increase in the other cost figures. In fact, some of the other cost factors declined.
We see, therefore, we can apparently produce the same amount of wealth with a considerably reduced working force. The same situation holds true practically over the whole picture of our industrial economy. We have an increase in productivity per man hour, and it has been fairly constant for many years, of about 2.5 per cent. This means that that, in itself, is a factor which must be compensated for by the expansion of our economy to take up the surplus labour force. It means, of course, that we are producing approximately the same amount of product with 97 per cent of the labouring force we have.
I believe these are the really serious aspects of the problem that faces us. It is true, as the minister stated, that the decline in gross national product can be accounted for by the -decline in farm production. It is true in fact that that decline in farm production accentuated the general economic difficulties, Increased the strain on our economy and no doubt sparked off this final rise of unemployment. But I believe we cannot comfort ourselves with the thought that all we have to do is wait for better crops in agriculture, and that in this way we are going to solve our economic problems; because I doubt very much whether the decline in farm income was the major factor in the decline we have been experiencing, because that decline had set in some time before the farmers on the western prairies were running into their difficulties.
I recall that last year I placed on the record the number of business failures for the two years preceding last year, and for last year, and I suggested that these were a warning signal to our government to which it should pay serious heed. Those signals are even more obvious this year than they were last, and more obvious in the last quarter of 1954 than at any time since 1939.
The business failures for 1952 were, in number, 1,512, and the total liabilities for that year were $29,652,000. In the following year, 1953, the total number of business failures had

risen to 1,657 and the total volume of liabilities had increased to $32,800,000. Then, in 1954, we had an increase up to 2,256 business failures with total liabilities of $53,047,000. Of that number of failures no less than 572 took place in the last three months of 1954. These, I suggest, are very grave warning signs for any government that purports to have the interests of the Canadian economy at heart. And you cannot dismiss them merely by taking a look through the rose-coloured spectacles of the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe), at his rose-coloured crystal ball, because I am afraid his reputation as a prophet is getting rather badly shattered; and if he is going to go on producing these documents there will be nothing left next year. Because prophets can make only a certain number of mistakes before people begin to wonder whether they are at the top of their profession as prophets.
I have mentioned the fact that I did not think the decline in farm income was a major factor in our present economic decline-and it is a definite economic decline. It is not one of the major factors accompanying the contraction in our economy. I do not think it was a major factor, because to some extent it has been compensated for by an increase in personal income in other sectors of the economy. In fact the net decrease in personal income from 1953 to 1954 was only some $36 million. But that underlines even more effectively the real problem facing us, and that is the problem of a contracting economy with an expanding population-an economy that not only is not standing still, but is definitely going backwards. And an economy such as that means that we are two steps away from prosperity. Because even if our production level and our capital investment level do remain constant, we would still be going behind because of the increase in our labour force, and the general increase in our population. And the process has been going on for some considerable time, despite the very rosy pictures painted to the house year after year from the government benches.
We have had a number of suggestions in the house as to how this problem should be dealt with. Certainly I would be very heartily in support of every suggestion that has been made. I think to deal with this urgent present problem-and it is an urgent present problem that has reached a volume which 20 years ago in the minds of the population of that time would have been considered a major disaster for the country-we should take steps immediately to increase the farm

income. We should take steps to relieve distress by a further expansion of unemployment insurance provisions and, of course, we should embark upon a number of badly needed public works in this country to take up the immediate slack in employment.
But I suggest that those in themselves are not really grappling with the problem we face, and that eventually, after we have completed them, we shall come out by the same door we went in. We shall still be facing the fact that the way we organize for production and distribution of wealth in this country does not enable us to go on expanding our economy and providing for a rising population.
When I was in Great Britain and Europe last year I heard a number of people expressing this point of view: They were rather disturbed by the fact that we in the western countries tend to concentrate our fears of the Soviet union and its satellites on the possibility of military aggression, whereas among the people in Great Britain and on the continent, who are by no means communists or socialists, there are many who express the fear that we may very well be facing a trade or commercial or industrial attack upon the economies of those countries. And they pointed out that the enormous expansion of the Soviet economy indicates that within a few years it will become a major factor in the world economy.
Of course people will say that the reason they are in that position can be traced to the quite horrible and deplorable conditions existing in that country. And that is perfectly true.
I do not think anyone would attempt to deny that that economic expansion has had really appalling social and political accompaniments. There are slave labour camps, undoubtedly, and there is tremendous oppression of the general public. But I think that is too easy an explanation of the manner in which the Soviet economy has been able to expand without the setbacks that continually have plagued the western economy. Whether we like it or not, I think we have to face the fact that, in spite of all these appalling accompaniments, they have got past the major obstacle confronting the expansion of private capitalist economies. As the minister pointed out the other day, they have got past the obstacle of declining markets, and of the fact that you have increased productivity and declining distribution of income on account of that increased productivity; and that when markets abroad begin to shrink, then the economy at home begins to contract.
I think we have to face the fact that they have got past that; and no matter how much we deplore and abhor the social and political
Unemployment
accompaniments of that economy, the very fact that they have got past this major obstacle does place them before us as a very major threat to our continued prosperity.
One of the quite striking features of this economy which, as I say, the people of Great Britain and of Europe fear may launch a still more disastrous attack on our way of life than can be launched in a military fashion, is that they do not have to rely upon external markets for a certain proportion of their production. Undoubtedly they do engage in export trade, and they have a purpose for it. But the purpose is diametrically opposed to the purpose we have in our export trade. Their export trade is designed merely tc provide them with the commodities they require for further extensions in their internal economy. And it is of course as a result of the fact that their economy is totally controlled and totally planned that there is no drain of profits which can be and are invested at the will of private individuals outside any concerted plan. They can be invested inside or outside a country such as Canada, where that is not the case in such an economy as the Soviet union.
I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that that is the serious question we have to face; that public works, unemployment insurance and aid to farmers are not solving this major problem; that the tremendous rise in productivity, the catastrophic effect on the living standards of a great many people of the automation, now called, that is proceeding so rapidly in North America, are going to present us with fundamental economic problems that we have to solve. It is quite useless to pretend in the first place that there are not nearly so many unemployed as we are led to believe, and to pretend in the second place that it is a temporary, accidental happening, because it is not. It is a perfectly inevitable, inexorable development from the way in which we produce goods.
I suggest that we are going to have to take a leaf out of the book of our potential enemy and do some planning in our economy; that we are going to have to have public activities, not merely in public works, but in productive enterprise. And that when we do that-and I do not think we are going to be able to avoid it; we already see the beginning right in this chamber of requests for massive public investments in such things as transcontinental pipe lines-we are going to have to continue in these sorts of activities. We are going to have to resort to investment in purely productive enterprise, and that is going to raise very serious problems for us, because either under private capitalism or under state capitalism, such as they have in the Soviet union, this development of mass

Unemployment
investment is going to be completely destructive of all democratic values in our society.
I suggest that, along with the solution to the economic problem which is present right now, we must start to see ways and means of controlling this modern development of collective public investment. We are not going to find it, Mr. Speaker, by following either the Russian pattern or the vast cartel organizations that are developing in the United States. We shall have to seek it, I think, on the co-operative road to salvation. These are the things that this house and this government should be seriously considering while they are at the same time taking the immediate steps that have been advocated here for the immediate alleviation of unemployment.
The other night I heard the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Johnston) accusing us in this group of having no program. I suggest there is no slick and easy program. What is required is a complete reassessment of our whole economic and political structure. That is required. We are not going to find a solution here by funny money, nor by lower taxation so that the owners of corporations would have more money to spend on trips to Bermuda. Nor are we going to find it by comforting ourselves by taking a little peek through the rose-coloured glasses or the crystal ball of the Minister of Trade and Commerce. We shall have to do some serious thinking and some serious discarding of prejudices and preconceived ideas, because we are up against the results, and they are quite shattering and appalling results, of human ingenuity in the production of goods and services.

I hope that some hon. members have been attempting to digest the analysis of the situation in which we find ourselves, which has just been given to the house by the hon. member for Nanaimo. I hope that his references to the progress which has been made in another part of the world will bring home to us, perhaps as effectively as the military threat which so many of us seem to consider all-important, the need to face up to the economic realities of life.
The debate in which we are engaged at the present time is one which we all recognize as an important one, although, to many of the people who have participated in it, it would appear that it consists largely of an argument on an analysis of certain statistics. To 
me that is the most ineffectual approach that we. can possibly take to the problem at the present time. As far as I am concerned, that is a kindergarten approach to the situation. It is perfectly true that we must have some knowledge of statistics, but even more important is what use we make of statistics when we have them.
Personally, I have no quarrel with the work which the Department of Labour has been doing in gathering the statistics. I do regret that the Minister of Labour appears to regard his function as being almost completed when his department has produced those statistics and when it has administered such things as the unemployment insurance fund. I would have hoped that from that department of our federal government there might come, in the light of what those figures reveal, a much more vigorous prodding in the direction of achieving some solutions than appears to have been the case up to the present time.

Mr. Speaker, when the house rose at six o'clock I was on the point of expressing my regret that the contribution which the Minister of Labour (Mr. Gregg) had made to this debate contained no evidence of any attempt to impress upon his colleagues in the government the seriousness of the situation which his own statistics revealed. I think if one were to consider the speeches made by the two ministers who have participated in this debate he could very well imagine himself in a university listening to a lecture on economics rather than in the Canadian parliament where at least some of us feel we should be making a serious attempt to bring about a more desirable state of affairs as far as employment activity in this country is concerned.
In view of the approach which some hon. members seem to have taken to this matter, perhaps it may not be out of place that we should consider ourselves as taking lessons in economics. I suppose if one grants to the members of the cabinet by virtue of their position the privilege of being the professors they will not resent too bitterly if some of the rest of us, whom they may regard as students, are not in complete agreement with everything they suggest.
I was interested in listening to some of the statements made by the Minister of Trade

and Commerce (Mr. Howe). For example, I find this on page 1629 of Hansard of March 1, 1955:
It is the concern of the government, as it is of all hon. members, to have unemployment at the absolute minimum consistent with the achievements of the essential goals of our economic life. In considering how these goals are to be achieved, it is, I think, essential that we examine carefully the current economic situation and our future prospects.
The minister spent some time examining the economic situation, but after listening to his speech and making a careful analysis of it later I must say that I am unable to find any mention of the goals to which he referred. Therefore I am somewhat at a loss as to just what goals he had in mind. Inadvertently or otherwise, the minister avoided mentioning any of those goals.
The fact that he omitted to suggest what these goals in our economic life should be ought to be recognized, I think, as lending considerable weight to the sort of comment which one hears all too frequently in lunch bucket conversations in many of our industrial plants, that in the view of this government the goal of our economy is to ensure that the pockets of the shareholders of our large corporations shall continue to be very well lined. The sort of approach which the Minister of Trade and Commerce took, I suggest, will simply lend weight to that suggestion which I am sure we could hear being uttered quite frequently if he went to the right places in this country. A little later on in his address the minister came as close as I could find to a suggestion of a goal. He said, as reported on page 1635 of Hansard:
A high level of employment in the Canadian economy can only be achieved by a program that will lift the Canadian economy as a whole to an extent that suitable employment for all types of workers can be made available.
I have read that statement two or three times and to me it adds up to saying that if everybody is employed there is no unemployment. That is as close to an expression of an economic goal as the minister came during the course of his remarks. As one who is only in his second session in this house that gave me a strange feeling that "that was where I came in."
I recall a somewhat similar debate which we had last year. As I recall, the remarks made by the Minister of Trade and Commerce during the course of that debate bore a remarkable similarity to some of the remarks which he made during this debate. The assurances that he gives us here he was giving us last year, this business of lifting the Canadian economy as a whole to an
