That is the program on which the government is engaged. The fact that the program is producing results will, I think, be made apparent to all during the next three or four months.
As I was saying, that seems to be similar to the things the Minister of Trade and Commerce was telling us a year ago, yet the statistics which were produced by the Minister of Labour indicate to what extent the program the Minister of Trade and Commerce had in mind a year ago has produced the results which he suggests will be produced within the next three or four months*
I was interested in discovering that the analysis made by the minister seemed to bear out a suggestion I had made during an earlier debate in which I suggested that the rate Of new jobs in this country was not keeping pace with the growth in the working force, that in fact somewhat less than 20 per cent of the increase in the working force during the past year had been absorbed into a proper place in our economic life. The minister said, as reported on page 1630 of Hansard:
In other words, during the past year or so employment has been maintained, but productive activity has not been sufficient to absorb the net increase in persons coming into the labour force.
And again, and I quote from page 1635 of Hansard:
The present level of unemployment is the result of known factors, which I have briefly attempted to outline. Knowledge of the causes has permitted us to act effectively within the proper sphere of governmental activities to meet the situation as it has developed.
It seems to me that as far as this government and its policy is concerned we are coming quite close to the crux of our problem. It is on the matter of what is the definition and the proper sphere of governmental activity that we come to the crux of the problem and find ourselves arriving at a situation such as we have at the present time. I feel that it is basically because of the fact that this government is extremely proud of being a "liberal" government. They are a liberal government in the sense of being the laissez-faire type of government that is actually living in the last century. That is the foundation of liberalism and that is the attitude which apparently this government cannot or will not outgrow. This question of what constitutes a proper sphere of governmental activity is, I think, at the very root of this problem in its relation to the activity of the government of this country. The government forgets that we are now in the middle of the twentieth century and that we are not living in the heyday of liberalism as

Unemployment
it existed in the time of my grandfather who was a good Manchester Liberal and who believed that the laissez-faire attitude which was current in the 1850's and the years following was the proper measure by which governmental activity should be set.
I feel this ties in with some of the remarks that were made by the Minister of Labour (Mr. Gregg) when he referred during the course of his speech to the measure to increase supplementary benefits under the Unemployment Insurance Act, as reported on page 1607 of Hansard for March 1, 1955. In this connection he said:
This in no sense meets the entire problem of unemployment which exists this winter. That problem will not be solved by waving a magic fairy wand over the country.
I certainly agree with that statement of the minister. He then went on to say:
It is not going to be improved by the introduction of controls in our economy at this stage, as was suggested by my hon. friend from Hamilton West.
And then occurred what was to me an interesting exchange, because the hon. member for Hamilton West (Mrs. Fairclough) rose immediately and said:
I shall have to rise on a point of order, Mr. Speaker. I did not mention controls at all. I referred to the levelling of orders.
Mr. Gregg then said he was sorry and the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming) said:
She said no such thing.
The hon. member for Hamilton West confirmed this by saying:
Not at all.
Then the hon. member for Eglinton, to make certain there was no question about it, said:
She said no such thing.
It would appear that so far as the Minister of Labour is concerned, and as far as those members who are sitting opposite him are concerned, this question of the introduction of controls or any form of regulation of the economy amounts to something which is considered to be a very naughty word. The moment one begins to talk about regulations somebody whispers, "Oh, that means regimentation," and that is an even naughtier word so far as they are concerned. I suggest, Mr. Speaker, when one talks about regulation or even regimentation, that it has a very different meaning to the people who are punching the time clocks in this country, and to the people who are engaged in the production lines of this monumental productivity about which we are so fond of talking.
The question of regimentation and regulation seems to have, I would suggest, a much

less serious note than some people in this house are inclined to describe it as having. The very essence of the productive process in which they are engaged is a form of regimentation and regulation. In the area in which I live there are four large industrial plants engaged in processing the products of the forests of British Columbia, and back of these industrial plants are a number of large logging camps which are engaged in the harvesting of the forest crops.
I wonder what would happen to the high productivity which those plants are able to create if all regulation and regimentation, if you care to use the latter word, were suddenly to come to an end. For example, if every man in that valley were given the right to decide when he wanted to go to work and when he wanted to stop work and whether or not he would go to work at all, you would have some of the workers, although probably not very many, coming in to work at 6.30 in the morning and some at 7.30 and others at 9.30 or 10.30. You would have some leaving for home at three o'clock in the afternoon and others at 2.30. I suggest that if regulation and an orderly management and control of that productive process were to be brought to an end, then the level of productivity in that area would sink to the point of the cottage industry era of earlier centuries.
I for one can see no reason why there should be considered to be a divine right not to be regulated for some people in this country, and why the mass of the people should be required to accept the form of regulation and regimentation which I have described.
This question of the regulation of the economy is an academic one to 95 per cent of the people in this country. The people who are unregulated are the small minority who have obtained for themselves more favoured positions in our economic situation. As far as I can see, there is no more logic in our having a planless economy in this country than there would be in having a planless productive process in the industrial plants to which I have referred.
I would suggest that, if we believe in democracy and in the democratic institutions which have been evolved throughout the centuries in the British tradition, there is no other alternative, if we are going to solve this economic problem, than that we try to use this democratically elected parliament and the government which is responsible to it as a means of bringing some form of over-all planning and control into our society.
It seems to me that, unless someone can produce a better suggestion as to how it can

be done, the time has come for our government to forget that it is composed of nineteenth century Liberals and to move into the twentieth century and accept the responsibilities of government which must come in the type of highly complex society in which we live today. I suggest the time has come when the government must revise its concept as to what constitutes a proper sphere of governmental activity.
I was interested in discovering that while the Minister of Trade and Commerce very carefully avoided any attempt to define what should be the economic goals of our economy there are some people in this country who have been giving some thought to this matter and indeed have been making some interesting statements in this connection.
One of these people is the president of the Royal Bank of Canada, Mr. James Muir. He terms 1955 as a year of decision in regard to the economic future of Canada. He makes this, to me, interesting statement. I would suggest, Mr. Speaker, that it is the kind of statement that even as short a time ago as ten years could not have been made by anyone except someone who was prepared to call himself a democratic socialist. These are Mr. Muir's words:
Within an over-all climate of political and economic freedom, our policy decisions in government and business during 1955 should take due account of four interdependent goals of an economic welfare of the community. The first of these is to ensure that our human resources are not wasted in involuntary idleness; that is, we should try to maintain a high and stable level of business activity and employment. The second goal is to ensure that our resources, when fully employed, are allocated in such a way as to produce the maximum volume of goods and services and to bring these goods and services to market in the proportions in which consumers want them. The third goal is to ensure that the distribution of the national product and income combines equity with the highest possible incentive to increase the total amount of product to be shared. The fourth and final goal is to ensure that all our policy decisions are consistent with an appropriate rate of economic progress and growth in the economy as a whole.
Mr. Speaker, on that statement of Mr. Muir's in an offhand way I would say there is some hope for him and that if he keeps on thinking in the terms in which he is at present thinking, perhaps in five years we may be able to welcome him into the ranks of the C.C.F. One of my colleagues suggests that if he wil1 bring all the money in the bank with him, we shall be quite happy to have him.
I would suggest that if these economic goals which have been outlined in this statement were to be taken seriously and if we in this parliament were prepared to get
Unemployment
down to the business of implementing measures to achieve the kind of goals that Mr. Muir has suggested, we should very shortly find ourselves discussing not the matter of unemployment but rather the question of a manpower shortage in this country. It seems to me that would be a much more appropriate subject for debate in this parliament of ours. It seems to me that it would be much more appropriate that we should be considering ways and means of finding the human resources to do the jobs we wanted to have done in order to provide the things we need.
It is not so difficult, if we take the words of the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) at their face value. He said that the present level of unemployment is the result of known factors. If it is the result of known factors, then apparently the only reason that it is not disappearing is that we are not properly applying our intelligence and our will to the solution of those factors that are known.
Just to give one example which necessarily perhaps is an oversimplification, let me say this. If our labour force in this country is 5 million people, and if through an increase in the productivity of those 5 million we find it is going to take 500,000 fewer people to do the same amount of work, and if the work week on the average, we will say, stands at 45 hours per week, it seems to me that it is a matter of a simple percentage calculation to determine how much the working week should be shortened; that is assuming, of course, that we are producing all of the things that we consider we need. We know those things but we do not use them.
It seems to me that it would be a proper sphere of governmental activity in this country to set the rules under which people work in the same way as the management in a plant sets the rules under which the people within that plant are going to work. But no; we do not do that. Instead of doing that, when we try to make the reduction in working hours that is possible because of increased productivity, we have to enter into a pitched battle between labour and management. Instead of doing the thing in an intelligent and orderly manner we find that the workers of the country are obliged to go out onto the picket lines and do battle.
In the lumber industry in British Columbia, how did the working week get shortened from 44 hours to 40? By a strike. How did the workers in that industry come to be able to enjoy some of their holidays with pay? Through a strike. People hold up their hands and say that working people should not

Unemployment
strike; , but they have no other alternative. Yet probably no one in this house would say that it is not. an absurd .and ridiculous situation when those things have to happen. In fact, the Minister of Labour (Mr. Gregg) says that the greatest ally in the maintenance of employment, and to bring about the fullest possible employment, is in the realm of good labour-management relations. Yet we sit back and leave that basic conflict between labour and management over how the benefits of increased productivity and improved technology are going to be passed on to the workers untouched. That would not be regimentation. That would be simply using good common sense.
There is another thing I wish to mention. Somebody this afternoon-I think it was the hon. member for Nanaimo (Mr. Cameron) - spoke of the question of what has come to be called automation. We perhaps do not realize how close some of the revolutionary effects of that process are upon us. We do not realize how quickly the aggravation of the result of that type of technological improvement is going to be with us. But even apart from that, even within the sphere of what is going on, it is evident to all of us at the present time that if these goals that the president of the Royal Bank of Canada has mentioned were being taken seriously and were being made the end of the policy of our government we would not have, for example, a situation that was drawn to my attention as the result of an arrangement that has recently been made to complete some houses on Vancouver island. The carpenters on Vancouver island, instead of dreading the fact that houses were going to be produced on an assembly line basis, could be welcoming that fact and that would be the sensible and proper thing for them to do. To me that is an illustration that comes close to home of the senselessness of the approach that our government continues to insist upon taking simply because, for one reason or another best known to themselves, they insist on living in a past era in regard to what they consider to be the proper sphere of governmental activity.
In closing, Mr. Speaker, may I say that I am quite happy to support this amendment that-
__the government should immediately give
consideration to the formulation of plans to deal with this emergency, and to the necessary steps to establish a long-term program for expanding employment to be presented to parliament during the present session.

On
January 19 of this year, Mr. Speaker, as reported at page 346 of Hansard, I used these

words during the debate on the address in reply to the speech from the throne:
What are the problems that face us today? Certainly by far the most important is unemployment. I agree with the Minister of Labour (Mr. Gregg) that there is no magic formula which can put an end to unemployment. But if unemployment were as regional and seasonal as the speech from the throne suggests, then I believe the magic formula of government handouts would do the trick. I am sure the Minister of Labour knows as well as we do that the situation now confronting us is much more serious than that. I know that in West York unemployment is greater today than it has been since the depression and I do not need the benefit of information from the dominion bureau of statistics to convince me of that fact.
Three weeks later, under dateline of February 8, the Canadian Press reported as follows:
Unemployment in the Toronto area has reached its highest point since the depression, G. S. Collins, manager of the local branch of the national employment service, said Monday. About 45,000 persons in the area, 8 per cent of the total working force, are registered for unemployment benefits, he said. This was about 10,000 more than last year's peak.
I am not going to enter into any controversy over the validity of figures; no matter from what source they come, they add up to a problem of extreme urgency. Let us be quite clear. Certainly, this is a problem that could be used by some for political advantage but I am sure that hon. members in this house sincerely believe that problems which affect the welfare of human beings, in a time of crisis, must be settled by co-operative action between all branches of government. Lest there be any doubt about the unanimity of opinion concerning this crisis, except of course amongst hon. members to your right, Mr. Speaker-if I take the hon. member for Spadina (Mr. Croll) as representative of that group, I would not know what they thought, because in the course of his short talk he indicated, first, that he agreed entirely with the Minister of Labour (Mr. Gregg); second, that he agreed entirely with my leader; third, that he subscribed entirely to the views of the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell). In fact, the only party he did not join in his 50-minute speech, although he did put some money in their pockets, was the group to your extreme left, for which I am sure they were truly thankful.
As an indication of the concern of all, I might quote from an editorial appearing in the Toronto daily Star on January 8 of this year. I need not mention that this paper is not usually out of step with the government. It reads in part as follows:
The speech from the throne offers welcome assurance that the federal government intends to take positive steps to deal with the growing

unemployment problem. There is to be a "substantial increase" in public works expenditures with a view of providing more jobs, and important changes are planned in the Unemployment Insurance Act to make it a "more effective instrument in providing financial support to unemployed workers". A stepped up public works program, properly planned and executed, can do much to relieve regional unemployment. But since unemployment today is fairly widespread, public construction should not be regarded as a solution of the problem.
Later, on February 9, in another editorial referring to the speech from the throne in the provincial legislature, the Toronto daily Star had this to say:
Ontario, along with the rest of Canada, has a serious unemployment problem. Welcome recognition of that fact is disclosed in the speech from the throne.
Then there is this:
At present, with both Ottawa and Queen's Park disclaiming responsibility, many jobless persons who are able and willing to work are left without public aid of any kind, causing great hardship to themselves and their families. The municipalities cannot afford to care for them.
In order to get everyone involved, the Liberal leader in Ontario is quoted as saying on March 1, 1955:
Primarily, unemployment is a municipal responsibility, but when that load becomes too great to bear then I say it is the responsibility of the province.
If the province were unable to cope with unemployment and then asked Ottawa for assistance, I would miss my guess if the federal government didn't give help then.
When I read all of these statements I certainly can see how the Financial Post can head its editorial "Seven Weeks Gone, Still They Talk". The editorial states in part:
If a trade association or a trade union or a church group of 260 people attempted to conduct its affairs as the House of Commons is doing, it wouldn't last a year. Its members would recognize its futility and quit.
I differ entirely with that paper's reason for its editorial, but in connection with the absolutely astounding line of thinking on the crystal ball basis that has emanated from the government benches in this debate, I believe we can only conclude that we could talk for seven weeks more with irresistible force and fail to budge the immovable object which is represented by the front benches to your right. But two things are plain. First, if the Minister of Labour still clings to the theory that unemployment is only regional and seasonal, then he has been and still is living in the ivory tower that he claims to disdain. Secondly, if the government cannot set aside for once its dogged determination to refuse to listen and call immediately for the conference my leader has proposed between federal, provincial and municipal
Unemployment
authorities, then I say the Winnipeg Free Press has exactly described this government when it said on June 6, 1954:
The present cabinet has by no means all the strength it used, to enjoy-there is in Ottawa a certain boredom, an overconfidence that leads to fumbling, a certain cynicism that bodes ill for resolute action, in a crisis.
There is no doubt that we are in a period of crisis. We in this party know the problem must be attacked on a twofold basis. To begin with, payments to people who are destitute can be only a poor substitute for a job, but the temporary solution must be found because I am absolutely convinced that the municipality, representing the home owners, cannot stand the burden of unemployment relief added to its expenditures on the restricted tax base it possesses. Educational and other costs since the war have necessitated increases in real estate taxes of 300 to 400 per cent in some cases. If you add unemployment relief on an ever-increasing scale to the top-heavy burden, lost homes can be the only result. People are out of work, not houses, and I fail, as I am sure every other member of this house does, to see how the home owner can carry any heavier burden.
A temporary solution is required to combat a most serious threat to our whole institution of government. We might as well face it: the communist party in this and every country throughout the world is preaching the philosophy of war boom and peace bust; it is a vulture waiting for the chance to strike. The ranks of the unemployed can become the battleground not only for men's stomachs, but also for their minds. Here it is-you all got your copy of their brief of February 28. See what they would hold out for you if you were unemployed. Listen to this:
Build 750,000 low-rental, low-cost homes, reduce down payments and mortgage interest.
And this:
Raise purchasing power and expand the home market-by higher wages and farm income; people before profits; a 7-hour day, 5-day week; repeal the sales tax; lower taxation on the people's homes, food and incomes, and higher taxes on corporation profits; a national health plan; payment of unemployment insurance benefits at 75 per cent of earnings for the full period of unemployment; old age pensions of $75 for men at 65, women at 60.
And this:
Improve the social and cultural life of Canada by building new schools, day nurseries, hospitals, theatres, recreational centres, sports stadiums, libraries, roads and highways.
And this:
Cut spending on armaments to the 1947 level, spend the money on people's needs. Ban the A and H bombs. Call for a conference of the great powers to preserve world peace and expand world trade.

Unemployment
Consider seriously if we can afford to wait one day longer, not seven weeks, to find a proper and equitable procedure to settle this problem. I might say to the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) that the same communist party must have received considerable comfort from his particular brand of boom and bust philosophy. I would like to read the condensation of an article which appeared in the Wall Street Journal of March 21. It says:
It is an absurd philosophy to believe that prosperity is made by government spending, and that if war spending stops prosperity will collapse. It is quite likely of course that if and when international tensions are eased there will be some decline in spending for war; but to conclude that this will be bad for a nation's economy is idiotic. Less government spending makes possible a lesser tax burden.
I say to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Harris) that our government has not done its part in reducing taxes to enable industry to convert to a strong peacetime economy. But what of the permanent solution to the problem? In this debate I have listened again to the complaints from our left that we in this party have not said what alternatives we propose, or what solution we have. You know, coming from that direction the complaint is a pretty hollow one.
It is much more difficult for us to suggest adequate alternatives than for the group to our left, because we do believe in the same basic system, Mr. Speaker, as hon. members to your right. And we must fit in any criticism we suggest into that same structure. But our hon. friends to our left are not so restricted. They have easy alternatives to every problem; total socialism in theory could move Gibraltar. In practice a pebble could present a major obstacle.
Then hon. members far to my left-they have no insurmountable problem, either. If we are short of money, we can supply a little "additive" income; or if we have unemployment we can take care of it with "unempay-ments".
Now, these words are not in the dictionary. But there is no problem in making up a few words, either. Frankly, the newspapers have been complaining about the lack of colour in our English in parliament, and the fact that it is no longer picturesque. Since the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) could use the expression, I think I can say, too, that all of these ideas from my left are cockeyed.
Just like you.

Unemployment
the crisis, the calling of a dominion, provincial and municipal conference of all tax authorities to explore ways and means of (.a)'' providing immediate additional cash ffelief for the unemployed without overburdening the home owner in his real estate taxes; (b) providing a program of public works construction to commence immediately to provide new jobs. Second, a long-range program to be tackled in partnership by management, labour and government to produce new jobs by (a) good hard work; (b) good now and unique sales techniques, basic designs and production methods; (c) improvements in the administration of government tp bring a reduction in taxes to be passed pp to. the producer and to put more purchasing power into the pockets of every citizen; (:d) realistic and aggressive approach to the specific problems raised by our participation in the GATT agreements; and (e) an end to the artificial exchange rate applicable to the Canadian dollar.
[. Only when we have attempted all of these things should we raise our heads and say we have done our best to whip the greatest problem which faces Canada today.

speakeroldname: Mr. F. G. J. Hahn (New Westminster):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as I listened to some of the government members talk in their mumbling way, calling "time", I thought how true it was that there were probably 600,000 electors in Canada who agree that it is time we had a, change in government. If there is to be a: change, I feel I might as well suggest that we should have a type of government that would be realistic in its approach. I suggest the one to which the hon. member for Spadina (Mr. Croll) referred yesterday when he said that British Columbia is contributing 80 per cent to the relief of unemployment and the municipalities 20 per cent and the federal government nothing.
I listened with considerable interest to the Hamilton plan, and I wondered why his party has not a party plan. One part of the Hamilton plan was enunciated the other day by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew) when he referred to the need for a dominion-provincial conference. Today the municipalities are being asked to take part in that conference also under the new Hamilton plan. I wonder just exactly how rapid a cure that would be for the immediate problem that is facing us at this time. I do not wish to devote any more time to the plan outlined by the hon. member for York West. I do wish to deal with what I have heard during the past two days, and more particularly I want to refer to what speakers for the government have said.

*As I look at them, I am reminded of what Walpole said on one occasion in a debate. He said that his policy was to let sleeping dogs lie. Ever since that time the British have been bungling through. Well, this government apparently has taken a lead from fhe British and they are still trying to bungle through and let sleeping dogs lie. The British have done so very effectively, but in this respect I would say they have become realistic a little more quickly about problems as they arise than we are willing to recognize.
Funny money.

The hon. member for Kootenay East speaks about funny money. I know of no man who is more capable of talking on that particular subject than the hon. member is. I am satisfied that one of these days he is going to get up in this house and make a speech and tell us all about funny money, what he knows about funny money. I am satisfied that when he is through he will probably go to the hon. member for Spadina (Mr. Croll) or he may even go to Mr. James Muir, the president of the Royal Bank of Canada, and ask how half a billion dollars in money was created for the building of the new homes that were put into existence in Canada this year. I would suggest that he take a lesson in funny money from some of the men who know something about the beginnings of money and how it is made. I would be quite ready to try to entertain him some day when I have more time, but I cannot do it at this particular time. I would suggest that the hon. gentlemen get next to someone who knows something about the making of money and he might learn a great deal about it.
As to unemployment itself, I would say that there is not a member of this house or any party represented in this house that does not feel there is a grave unemployment problem facing the people of Canada today. However, I have been rather taken aback by hearing some of Canada's foremost citizens devote so much of their valuable time, when they are speaking to this subject, quote figures to prove a statement which we know is a fact and have known for some months.
I do not care whether there are 500,000 unemployed, whether there are 200,000 unemployed or whether there are 100,000 unemployed. As long as there are men and women who are facing the trials and tribulations that we have to face in Canada today, who are desirous of obtaining a job and who need a job in order to exist, then it is time that we looked into our economic system to see whether we might not create some of the funny money that was proposed yesterday by the hon. member for Spadina.

A good number of Canadian citizens are hungry today; a good number of them wish to sell the labour of their hands or the product of their minds, but they cannot do so because they cannot find a buyer. The quack remedies that we have been subjected to during the past few years are beginning to fail. The regular Liberal spring tonic is failing this spring as a tonic for seasonal unemployment. Time has caught up with this disease of unemployment, the disease that has been prevalent since 1929 and which we have said so frequently was taken out of our hands by Adolf Hitler.
I followed the debate quite closely and I have read much about it. In order that I may not be biased, I am going to turn to the newspapers for support of what I am going to say. Among other things I discovered that my socialist friends to my immediate right propose a twelve year plan. That is not uncommon among socialists because in Russia they have a five year plan.
You have no plan.

The hon. member says that we have no plan. We have a plan which was proposed in this house on two separate occasions. We have an immediate stop-gap for the present condition and we have an over-all plan in finance that will take care of unemployment for all time, not just for the present.
The problem with which we are faced is an immediate problem and the dominion-provincial conference proposed by the Conservatives will be of no value to the men and women who need help at this time. In her gracious way the hon. member for Hamilton West (Mrs. Fairclough) explained to us how grave the situation was and proposed the amendment which made it possible for us to carry on this particular debate.
The Minister of Labour (Mr. Gregg) is always concerned with problems of this type. Apparently he had some debate with his conscience. As he went along with his speech he claimed that this was a provincial responsibility. I disagree completely with him. This government, this parliament, this federal authority deprives the provincial and municipal authorities of the simplest means of producing revenue. We have under our control the means of sustaining production; we have control of the financial institutions within our country; we formulate trade policies which so clearly reflect the employment picture. Then the Minister of Labour tells us that it is the responsibility of the provincial governments.
I am satisfied that he does not believe that in his own mind, but possibly this is the "out" that the government has been looking for.
Unemployment
The leader of the C.C.F. attempted to prove that unemployment is directly related to farm income.
He proved it.

The hon. member says, "He proved it". If you talk to labouring men and industrialists you will find that they believe, and possibly rightly so, directly the opposite. But I would agree with one point which he raised, that the best answer to communism is to have full stomachs across Canada every night. If we have that we shall not have to worry about the threat of communism.
We have been saying that for years.

There is no hon. member in this house who does not believe the same thing, yet we are told it is C.C.F. policy. I am merely stating a matter of fact. The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) agreed with that wholeheartedly. He was possibly the most enthusiastic supporter of the leader of the C.C.F. when he said that we have to bring up farm prices. I know the Minister of Agriculture well enough to say that.
They say it but they do not do anything about it.

That is true. Possibly their policy may not permit that, but at the same time the fact remains that you cannot claim it as your policy. All these wonderful things that we hope for the men and women of this country do not form part of your policy only.
The Minister of Trade and Commerce indicated a desire on the part of the government to forestall criticism. I would say that that was the reason for his taking part in this debate. It is one of the first occasions on which we have had the privilege of hearing two ministers early in a debate. It indicates one of two things. Either the government feels in its own mind that this problem is of such vital importance to the nation that we should have a policy outlined and a statement made by the man who controls trade, or they wanted to forestall criticism. It was a carefully prepared statement which lacked the zip which the minister is ready to put into ordinary things. It was carefully thought out and I compliment him upon it.
However, he did prove to me quite conclusively that there is no interdependence between Canada and the United States. Without interdependence of trade between Canada and the United States we are on a one-way street. We are completely dependent upon it. If we do not have that market then apparently we are going to suffer the pangs of hunger and unemployment. Of course, the

Unemployment
Right Hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) has a cure for these things. He has a cure for everything. His cure is an optimistic smile with a simple cure-all of "a highly productive low cost efficiency." I would agree with him that if we can get what he wants, a highly productive low cost efficiency, it would help under the present circumstances. We had that efficiency and that low cost productivity before 1930 and yet we do not have it at the present moment. We possibly can get it, however, and we will get it in the not too distant future.
There are other minor and major causes of unemployment. Before we can find a cure we should know what these particular causes are. While some of them appear quite minor and somewhat localized their effect is felt over the whole nation and they should be taken into consideration in order that we might find some means of offsetting them.
One of these causes is the effect of strikes. I do not wish to give the impression that I am opposed to strikes. The right to strike is perhaps the only means by which the working man can get the result he feels entitled to. I dare say, however, that the strike in Windsor with a relative loss of payroll affected the purchasing power of possibly over 70,000 persons within this country for a period of three months. That is a considerable number of people to add to our staggering list of unemployed. It represented a loss of purchasing power which is so vital to the nation as a whole.
Another cause which I found so prevalent on the Pacific coast just prior to Christmas is the plea which merchants used in then-advertising, "No down payment". Possibly if there had been no down payment but payments were required to commence the following month conditions would not be so alarming as they are at present on the Pacific coast so far as the merchants and their staff are concerned. However, certain unscrupulous merchants, and I use the word advisedly, deliberately made statements over the radio to the effect that no down payment was required on particular articles in the month of December or the latter part of November. The advertisement said in effect, "You do not have to pay on January 1; you do not have to pay on February 1; but pay on March 1." Well, Mr. Speaker, this is March 1-

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: This is March 3.
Free enterprise.

That is exactly what was done by free enterprise, as my friend suggests.

We can make regulations in respect to payments that will take care of that very easily and it is free enterprise. I think you should study your books.
Now, that is a very important point and it certainly had its relative effect upon the markets of the Pacific coast and other places where the same policy was followed.
There is a third cause which is minor and in which the Minister of Finance (Mr. Harris) may be interested. As a businessman I have found it affects wholesalers, retailers and consumers. It particularly affects them at this time. I found in my travels, and I think if you were to discuss it with the retailers, wholesalers and consumers you would find it is true. Perhaps some of the hon. members find themselves doing it also. It is at this time when the budget is released in Canada people generally automatically wonder, "Can we expect a cut in taxes on a particular item so that we will save that amount?" Let us examine the picture as it stands today. The government has announced no increased expenditures. We can naturally assume therefore that the amount of revenue required is not going to increase. This also means that we are not going to increase taxes. If we do not increase taxes we can hope they will decrease. This will affect the sales within the nation. That will have a material effect upon a certain number of unemployed people not in an individual community but across the nation as a whole. While the number of people who are affected may not be too many, at the same time their earning power is reflected upon every individual in the nation.
There is a fourth cause which affects unemployment and that is automation. I do not intend to deal with that at this time, however, because it is self-evident. If time permits I shall have something to say about it later.
I looked in vain for cures suggested by some of our good friends. I feel the proposals contained in six different points outlined by the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Johnston) should receive the attention of this government in so far as he proposed an immediate cure for the unemployment condition which exists today.
I believe that we have to find an immediate cure. The government has indicated its inability to cope with the problem. The government is not alone in this regard. Our socialist and Conservative friends have called for a dominion-provincial conference and public works program. While that may be something which will have value in the future it is not something which offers an immediate

solution to the problem. This government has ridden the crest of prosperity to a nonexistent oasis and is left stranded in the desert groping like a man who has gone sand blind, bewildered and befuddled and unable to find the obvious route to freedom. The government is behind the proverbial eight ball and is trying to find a way out. I do not blame it if it does not have the answer. We in this group think we do have the answer. We are satisfied that it deserves considerable attention, more than the government has been prone to give it in the past. As I said earlier, it is only because this thing was a dead issue that no one was prepared to listen to us. Today, however, we find that a good number of men in the financial field are willing and ready to give our solution considerable thought and study.
I wish to return to the statement made by the hon. leader of the C.C.F. (Mr. Coldwell) that unemployment bears a direct ratio to farm prices. Might it not also be said that the price of farm produce is directly affected by full employment. If the people in this country have money with which to buy consumer goods the prices will go up. Is it not true that Adam Smith's principle of supply and demand still holds true and that if people have money with which to buy food and if they want food the price of that food will increase. That is the point of view of the labourer. You C.C.F. people say you are for labour and the farmers, yet you are not ready to recognize labour's needs. The question is, which came first the chicken or the egg?
They are interdependent.
I am glad you recognize that now.

We
have been saying that for years.

I am glad to hear that.
Well, during the war we had full-time employment and that of course was reflected in a stabilized farm price. The basic weakness today is the shortage of consumer dollars. This of course is reflected in conditions as they exist today.
We presently have social welfare legislation, which, thanks to the present government, is helping considerably to offset a drastic situation such as we went through in the thirties. I do not believe there is an hon. member in this house who would say that, if it were not for unemployment insurance, war veterans' allowances, family allowances, old age pensions and old age security, instead of having 600,000 unemployed we would have well over 800,000 unemployed. These things
Unemployment
have done one thing if nothing else. They have deterred our plunge into economic chaos more than has any other factor this government has instituted. I say that it is important to inject purchasing power into the hands of the consumer who lacks that purchasing power.
This matter of automation that I spoke of earlier is a problem that is with us now but to a lesser degree. It is being accepted and it is going to be accelerated. This field of electronics that we have today is going to play a vital part in cutting down the labour force required in the near future. Possibly it is a matter that would fit in well with what the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) suggested in his 12-year plan. But certainly it is something that must be considered. We find factories that are operated today with practically one-quarter of the staff they needed ten years ago. Through the field of electronics we find such things as the ability, by electronics, to take out of the sea fish of a particular length and of a particular species, by using different propulsions.
This matter of stiff competition is going to bring in more efficiency. That was the statement of the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) when he suggested that may be the answer to the problem. Automation will bring in that efficiency but it will throw more men out of work. We must not become the slaves of machines. Machines must be made to work for us. We must find the answer to the problem. If the only way in which we can create money to pay these people so that they can buy goods is by having them work, then we are going to be in a sorry plight in the not too distant future. Labour must be made to learn, as must the rest of society, that this thing is here and that it is here to stay. It is going to be improved upon. Possibly in the not too distant future we are going to have a 36-hour week, then a 30-hour week and possibly even a 20-hour week. But we are going to have to get out of those machines enough wealth, paid in the form of tickets, money or dividends or whatever you want to call it, so as to make it possible for the people to purchase the commodities that are made.
There are certain immediate curatives that I want to refer to again as outlined by the members of the group that I represent. I am not going to deal with each one of them because I have not the time in which to do so. Two or three of them were dealt with by other members quite efficiently and possibly much better than I might be able to deal with them. However, there are one or two that I want to speak about. The

Unemployment
first is the elimination of the sales tax and wider use of price discount.
Time.
Is somebody suggesting time for a change again?
Time.
He is just talking through his hat.

As to the wider use of the price discount, that, of course, was instituted in the case of butter and milk. This is an immediate cure. I do not want this as a long-range cure, but it is an immediate cure for the unemployment situation. The saving in sales tax alone would amount to approximately $417 million. That is a form of dividend which might be brought back into the hands of the people and which would immediately give them purchasing power. Thus the unemployed would find that they are able to purchase the goods that they so badly require.
Time.

The second factor is that the federal authority should assume full responsibility for financial assistance to the unemployed who are not now covered by unemployment insurance. On that matter, I would propose that we expand the war veterans allowance, the family allowance, the old age pension, and old age assistance. In this particular case I would say this. There is no value in our putting any more money in the hands of those who have more money than they can spend at this time. There is no value in giving an old age pension to a man who today has an income which is large enough to keep him and his family well. The person who requires it is the man who is unemployed. He is the individual who should reap the benefit of this increase that we might propose. That is why, when I spoke on the address in reply to the speech from the throne, I proposed that we should have a complete review of this social welfare field in order to see where it is possible to make a form of redistribution so that none of us are starving while others are living in affluence.
We should have a vigorous employment policy with government assistance to private enterprise. The purpose of this suggestion is to absorb seasonal employment. Last year I had the pleasure of introducing a housing scheme which I thought would be of considerable value. I referred to it as the Brazilian housing scheme. I refer to it again. I am not going to take the time of the house to review the matter again. At the time I spoke on it the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Winters) said that he had not heard of

it. I do not know whether or not he has bothered to examine into it any further. However, I would recommend it to the financial experts on the other side of the house who are looking for money in order to put these unemployed to work. It was done in Brazil; and I am satisfied that we should be able to do equally well anything the coffee raisers in Brazil could do.
I now come to the remarks made by our friend the hon. member for Spadina (Mr. Croll) who once again proved himself to be the humanitarian that he is by drawing to our attention the plight of the unemployed. I was glad to hear him say that this is the place which has responsibility for the unemployed. I agree with him-these were not his words; I use my own-that the payment of insurance is a subsistence allowance and not a matter of creative dollars. I am satisfied that he is quite right in that respect. The need is urgent for the creation of dollars to be used in the creation of enterprise which creates more work. We should not be trying to get work for work's sake. If that was the desire, we could give everybody a teaspoon, send them out on the trans-Canada highway and say, "We will give you a dollar for a day's work" or $5 or $10. That should not be the question.
Time.

The question is this, Mr. Speaker. People want work and they want it badly. If the hon. gentleman opposite has something to say, I will give him 40 minutes after I have finished. He is entitled to it. In the meantime, let him please listen. If he does not want to listen, there is a lobby in which he can sit.
You have nothing to say.

I would make a further suggestion in connection with this question and that is in the case of housing. I am satisfied that the housing program as outlined today, has just about reached, or probably will within a three-year period reach, the point of satiation. The families that were raised in the thirties were small. New home owners are decreasing in number, or the number who are becoming eligible for new homes is decreasing. But there is a huge field that remains untouched. That field is with respect to the man or home owner of today who has built a two-room, t'nree-room or four-room home. It is his home but it is small. It is too small for his family. He built it just shortly after the war when there was no place he could go. He had $1,000 or $2,000. He has spent

his money in building a very small home, and today he needs help to enlarge it.
Now, there we have one of the biggest potential sources of employment for the seasonal unemployed. Some of these men are possibly unemployed at this time. They may be in the lower wage groups, but they are heavy users of durable goods. In this instance I should like to pass on a compliment to industry in my own area. It has seen fit to make it possible for this small home owner to borrow up to $2,000 repayable within a two-year period. It is unfortunate that the industrialist cannot extend credit for 20 or 30 years, as our government is in a position to do through the banks. These men are good risks. Industry recognizes that they are good risks. Although they are good risks, the loan must be repaid within two years because industry must renew its capital. They have to get back some of that money to put it to work over again. The important fact is that the interest rate is too high, the carrying charges are too high and the repayment period is too short. I sincerely ask the government to consider the possibility of making loans of up to $2,000 available to these home owners who wish to improve their homes. I would say that in probably every metropolitan area within this dominion there are such needy people. Such a step would help to look after the home owner and the unemployed in Toronto, Montreal, Vancouver or wherever they may be.
When the hon. member for Spadina (Mr. Croll) suggested the creation of new money, we applauded. He said that he was getting his applause from the wrong side of the house. Why should we not applaud? After all these years we have finally got someone on the other side of the house to recognize the fact that the creation of money is not going to ruin our credit, ruin the value of our dollar. After all these years, we have finally got someone over there who has started talking a little sense instead of referring to funny money and calling "time". I am rather hopeful that he will explain this to his colleagues, and that the government will give it careful consideration. Then, we will have some of these members who are always calling "time", and are so anxious to run off to their homes in Quebec, ready to listen to ordinary sense and reason in the matter of finance. This would enable us to put this house of ours in good order.
The president of the Royal Bank of Canada does not take that view of funny money. I should like to propose once again that these hon. gentlemen go to him and ask him how the money was created with which we built
Unemployment
homes during these past years. One of these days we will explain the story again. Probably it has been explained once each year for the past 20 years. Now, an increase in capital investment for the creation of enterprise could be used to help our Canadian economy and thereby help the people who are today unemployed. I would suggest low cost loans on a long-term basis for such things as the establishment of homes or industries. In so far as cyclic production is concerned, the loans could be made on a shortterm basis.
The construction of national projects, such as our Minister of Public Works (Mr. Winters) has seen fit to plan throughout the country, should be carried on in the winter months when unemployment is at its worst. Governmental money could be spent at the time when it would do the most good. Under those circumstances, I would not say we should necessarily stop production during the summer because we would probably find ourselves with unemployment in the summer months, but we should save governmental projects for the winter months because that is the traditional period of seasonal unemployment.
I would suggest that if it is at all possible, in those areas such as Toronto, Vancouver and the Pacific coast we should build the shell of the building during the summer months and leave the finishing until later in the winter. I know that would not be possible in all circumstances, but certainly it holds true in a great many. I would further suggest that we continue these public works projects on a provincial-federal co-operative basis.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. I am sorry to interrupt the hon. member but I am afraid I must advise him, and this is with authority and accuracy, that his time has expired.

great deal has already been said in this house since this debate on unemployment started. Many views have been expressed, some rather absurd and some rather inconsistent. The hon. member for Hamilton West (Mrs. Fair-clough) led off the debate by quoting columns of figures and percentages with which most of us were familiar. The Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) has given us a comprehensive list of reasons for the business slump resulting in unemployment for the 'atter part of 1953 and 1954. He has pointed jut also to the house his reasons for believing that there has been an upturn in business. Those factors relating to the upturn are ones that simply cannot be disregarded. I am not

Unemployment
going to recount them, but nevertheless the undisputed facts are still there.
During the past few weeks the employment situation in Hamilton has shown some improvement as indicated by a decline in registrations at the national employment office. On January 28, 1954, the number of applicants registered at the national employment office in Hamilton totalled 12,731. On February 8 of last year they were 12,911, an increase. This year, on January 27, there were 15,485 registered at the national employment office. On February 17, 1955 the total was 14,717. From January 27 to February 17, there was a decline of about 770 in the number of job applicants. This was a result of gradual recalls in a number of industries in that area, the largest being the Steel Company of Canada. The Firestone Tire and Rubber Company are back on full-time operations or expect to be in the very near future. The outlook for employment in Canadian Westinghouse has also improved during February with the securing of two large orders for heavy electrical equipment.
Now, let us face other facts that we should face fairly and squarely. Either we are going to maintain a system of free enterprise, one in which the government should do everything within its power to encourage the development of initiative and investment in industry, or we should follow the policy of government control, centralizing and nationalizing all our private industries. This is the policy of my socialist friends which undoubtedly would lead to the taking away of our individual freedoms.
You would like to have unemployment.

My hon. friend from Broadview (Mr. Hees), the rich poor man's friend, has stated that we must open steel mills in the west, that we must develop hydroelectric power and provincial services, that we must build up secondary industries in Canada. I wonder who should do this, in the opinion of my hon. friend. Certainly it is a fine principle; but surely these things must come about by free enterprise.
After listening to the opinions of those opposite, if we are to believe them, then the whole country is evidently headed for ruin. If private industry faced the future today with the same attitude as my hon. friends across the way, it is a wonder that they would consider the investment of one five-cent piece, or have any confidence whatever in the future of Canada.
Just because the government of the day is confident of an upturn in business, which is substantiated by the Minister of Trade and

Commerce (Mr. Howe), there is no reason why the same government cannot recognize the seriousness of the present unemployment situation; and they are recognizing it. The very fact that we are debating unemployment at this time substantiates what I have said.
The hon. member for Broadview told us today-and while I do not have his exact words, this is very close to what he said- that "the government is perfectly satisfied and intends to do nothing about it". How a supposedly competent member of parliament could honestly make a statement of that kind is more than I can understand. The Minister of Trade and Commerce has given us the government's formula for a better 1955, beginning with tax reductions, cheaper money, and the other means that he enumerated.
I have not heard one member in the opposition come out and say flat-footedly that all tariffs should be raised. But I want to tell you that most of the measures adopted by this government are along the lines of those suggestions made to the government by labour and management alike. I am not suggesting that the policy was adopted because of these suggestions, but I am saying that labour and management concur in this prescription.
Let me say this: We sit here and listen to contradiction after contradiction from the opposition. Some suggest that a reduction in cprporation taxes should be made. Others suggest a lowering of income tax, while others suggest the abolition of the sales tax. Where is all the money to come from to build the trans-Canada highway that the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) would like to build? Where is the money to come from to raise family allowances, old age pensions and veterans allowances? Where is the money to come from to build power developments, to clear slums and to build low rental housing developments?
I was very interested in the arguments advanced yesterday by the hon. member for Spadina (Mr. Croll) when he urged the government to take positive action in the clearance of slum areas, and to build low rental housing. In my opinion each and every member in the house has been very shoddy in his own responsibility, where a situation such as that described by the hon. member exists. Surely no one is so naive as to suggest that the federal government should proceed to buy or to expropriate slum areas and to build houses without consulting the provinces or the municipalities.
Why, we are already accused of running a bureaucracy. Who is in a better position to judge what is needed in this regard than

the member in the House of Commons representing his constituency? Who is in a better position than a member of parliament to go to the municipal government and say, "Here is a small area that should be cleared out. Let us go to the federal government and arrange for low cost rental housing." Who is in a better position than the member of parliament who sits in the House of Commons to do that very thing? You will not find our government turning down a proposal of this kind, if the request is made by the municipality, and if that request is a sound one.
But it will do no good to shout across this chamber, "Let us do this" or "Let us do that". I say: Let us go out and take some initiative ourselves. Let us show some leadership for a change, instead of being arm-chair generals, and just sitting in the House of Commons and discussing it.
Let me give an example of what I mean. In the city of Hamilton we have approximately 470 wartime houses that were to have been demolished or removed as of July 1 of this year. This was brought about by an agreement between Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation and the city council of Hamilton, when the city insisted upon their removal. I met the mayor of Hamilton and one of the controllers, and we agreed to make an effort to help these 470 families who were faced with eviction.
What did we do? We got together with the officials of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation and the provincial authorities in Toronto and came up with a plan. If I may be permitted, I should like to read from the Globe and Mail of March 1, where I find this:
A plan to solve one of the city council's biggest headaches-removal of 470 wartime houses on the mountain-and to provide low rental housing was outlined here late this afternoon. Details of the plan were revealed by Mayor Lloyd Jackson and A. E. K. Bunnell, provincial housing administrator, at a press conference. The plan calls for the moving of the 470 wartime houses from their present location on the mountain to 70 acres of land north of Mohawk road and east of Wentworth street.
The project, to cost an estimated $2,500,000 will be financed under the National Housing Act with the federal government paying 75 per cent, provincial government 171 per cent and municipal government 71 per cent.
Each house will be placed on a permanent foundation, with a new gas or oil furnace, will be renovated inside and out to meet present building standards and the property will be landscaped.
Mayor Jackson said the project will give Hamilton 470 low rental homes. Under the present plans the houses are to rent for $45 a month.
People with families and with incomes of $40 to $65 a week will have preference. Families now living in the wartime houses who can qualify will be given first chance to occupy the houses.
Mayor Jackson said the plans were originated and worked out by Controller Jack MacDonald
Unemployment
and Russell Reinke, M.P. for Hamilton South. The two have been working on the project with the assistance of the mayor for several months.
Tenants of the wartime houses have been given notice to vacate the homes by July 1. This date was set last fall when council decided to live up to its agreement to remove the wartime houses.
This was no easy task; but I found our government most co-operative. I do not know how far-reaching the effects will be in so far as employment is concerned; but I am sure of one thing: we will not spend $2,500,000 on a housing- development in the city of Hamilton without giving work to a great number of people. We did not sit back and wait for parliament to open so that we could come here and express our views in idle chatter, such as we have heard in the house in the last three days. I am not suggesting that I deserve the credit; but I do say that all persons co-operated.
If each of the 265 members in the house put forth more constructive efforts, and were a little less destructive, we would have less unemployment today.
Now, Mr. Speaker, a word about one phase of unemployment that must be faced and faced now, namely, the problem of the unemployed employables. I hold in my hand a telegram from the chairman of the public assistance committee of the council of community services. The hon. member for Hamilton West (Mrs. Fairclough) read the same telegram to the house the other day; therefore I shall read only a part of it, to this effect:
Seventeen thousand dollars spent by city in January and nearly that much in February for unemployed employables without benefits and needing emergency relief.
What is happening? The city of Hamilton cannot stand by and watch these people starve, and so they must provide the necessary assistance. Fathers are leaving their families so that the families may qualify for assistance. The Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew) has urged the government to call an immediate tax conference with the provinces. How absurd that is. Even if the conference could be called tomorrow, he knows that all ten provinces could not meet immediately without any preparation; and even if they did meet right away a formula could not be adopted overnight that would be acceptable to all.
Let me read from an editorial in the Globe and Mail of Wednesday, March 2, 1955:
Ontario is ready and willing to accept the 1954 proposals of the federal government for dealing with unemployment, Premier Frost yesterday told a delegation of the Ontario provincial federation of labour.
The province has told Ottawa this, the premier said, and the Ontario government also has repeatedly expressed the view that any solution

Unemployment
to the unemployment problem must be a cooperative one. All levels of government must share the responsibility, he declared.
The premier of Ontario tells us that any solution to unemployment must be a co-operative one, which is quite true. But what has happened? As I stated before, in January, 1955, the city of Hamilton paid out $17,000 for the unemployed employables. In that same month the total amount paid out in the form of unemployment insurance was $811,516. You say that unemployment insurance is contributory. That is perfectly true. It is contributed to by the employer and the employee. While that is true, do not forget that the government contributes one-fifth to this fund. In the case of Hamilton, the contribution of the federal government to this fund of $800,000 would amount to approximately $140,000 in the month of January. In addition, our estimates this year to maintain employment offices across Canada amount to $27 million. And yet someone has the audacity to say that we are not spending money. Our contribution to the unemployment insurance fund will amount to $32,500,000 in the next year. What is the province contributing? Where is this sharing of responsibilities that Mr. Frost speaks about?
Here is another point. The larger group of the unemployed are those who have no trade or profession. Consequently, this government has provided legislation to give vocational
training to the unemployed and to equip them for better positions. The federal government will pay 50 per cent of the cost of this vocational training of the unemployed and the province 50 per cent. Has the province of Ontario come forward to help train our unemployed under this plan? Not on your life. Here again, where is the co-operation? It seems to me that most of the provinces in Canada today have a budget surplus, and yet they leave the responsibility for the unemployed employables to the municipalities. It seems to me that all the initiative in the past has been left to the federal government. Well, let us show them that we do not mind taking the initiative once again, as we have done in the past.
On motion of Mr. Ellis the debate was adjourned.
